questions_now.q: Do people describe ketamine trips the way others describe near-death experiences?
Do people describe ketamine trips the way others describe near-death experiences?

lines_now.short: Of 165 drugs, ketamine trip reports used words most like accounts of near-death experiences. Salvia and LSD came close behind.
lines_now.but: Only words were compared. Nobody showed the trips and the near-death experiences feel alike.
how: Researchers took about 15,000 drug reports from the Erowid website. A computer compared their words with 625 near-death accounts.
With the main settings, ketamine came first. Averaged over all settings tried, it led LSD only narrowly, and other drugs swapped places.
The near-death accounts were written about 20 years after the event. Nobody checked what the online writers took, or how much.
Some think a brain chemical like ketamine causes near-death experiences. The authors say their study cannot show that.
lines_now.rate: One study comparing words in reports people chose to post online with near-death accounts written years later. Nobody checked the drugs, and ketamine's lead over LSD was small.

claim.statement: In about 15,000 written reports of drug experiences on the Erowid website, covering 165 substances (reports of combinations left out; all reports for each substance merged into one document; drug names, slang and words for routes deleted), compared with 625 written accounts of near-death experiences that people gave voluntarily to research groups in the USA and Belgium (also merged into one document), reports about ketamine, compared with the reports about each of the other 164 substances, are associated with the pattern of word use most similar to the near-death accounts, as scored by a text-mining method (latent semantic analysis) that gives one similarity number per substance, with no measure of uncertainty and no check against questionnaires about experiences (Martial et al., 2019). Nobody was given a drug or interviewed for this study. With the main settings (20 dimensions), ketamine scored about 0.90 on a 0-to-1 scale, against about 0.84 for Salvia divinorum and about 0.83 for peyote and for LSD (values the editors read from a figure); averaged over all the settings tried (5 to 145 dimensions), ketamine led narrowly, about 0.64 against about 0.61 for LSD and about 0.60 for psilocybin mushrooms, and it came first with about 4 in 5 of the settings (read from a pie chart), LSD with most of the rest. Rankings made with very different settings agreed poorly below the top: peyote, third with the main settings, was about 18th on the average. When the near-death accounts were split by cause, closeness to death or how pleasant they were, ketamine stayed first in almost every subset; after cardiac arrest, LSD ranked comparably. As classes, dissociative drugs ranked first, then deliriants and serotonergic psychedelics, with sedatives, stimulants and antipsychotics or antidepressants lowest. Similar word patterns are not shown to be similar experiences: the score counts how words occur together (a word such as fear counts whether it was felt or denied, as the authors note); the near-death accounts were written on average about two decades after the event, and 30% were attributed to anaesthesia or drug use (cause missing for 228 of 625; the base of the percentage is not stated); the Erowid writers, their doses and settings are unknown and the substances were not tested; and the authors state that their analysis neither validates nor refutes neurochemical explanations of near-death experiences, such as the idea that the brain releases a ketamine-like chemical near death, although their abstract says the results support that speculation and suggests ketamine could be a safe and reversible experimental model of near-death experiences, which was not studied. Funded by public research bodies and private foundations; two of the 12 authors are at the Erowid Center, which curates the reports; no conflict-of-interest statement is printed. Certainty: very low. Status: single study.
claim.population: Two existing collections of written reports, merged by substance: (1) about 15,000 reports from the Erowid Experience Vaults, a curated website holding more than 20,000 reports written by people who chose to submit them, on 165 substances with more than 10 single-substance reports each (demographic information on the writers not commonly available; the authors call the population relatively homogeneous culturally; doses and settings unknown); (2) 625 retrospective narratives (623,926 words) of near-death experiences given in an anonymous voluntary questionnaire to the Division of Perceptual Studies, University of Virginia Health System (USA), and the Coma Science Group, University and University Hospital of Liège (Belgium), all scoring 7 or more on the NDE Scale except 182 collected before the scale existed; 68% women; mean age 31 (SD 15) at the experience and 52 (SD 13) when the account was collected; cause attributed to head injury 13%, anaesthesia or drug use 30%, cardiac arrest 10% (228 missing)
claim.exposure: Reports about ketamine, as named by their writers (substance, dose and route not verified; route words deleted from the texts)
claim.comparator: Reports about each of the other 164 substances, ranked against one another; no collection of other kinds of experience was compared
claim.outcome: Similarity of word use between each substance's merged reports and the merged near-death accounts: the correlation of reduced term-document columns after tf-idf weighting and latent semantic analysis (20 singular values in the main analysis, 5 to 145 in robustness checks); the resulting ranking of substances and of drug classes
claim.magnitude: Martial et al. (2019) print no values, intervals or tests for the ranking itself. Main analysis (20 singular values; Fig. 3, editors' measurement of dot centres at 600 dpi, approximate): ketamine 0.90, Salvia divinorum 0.84, Lophophora williamsii (peyote) 0.83, LSD 0.83, 5-MeO-DMT 0.83, psilocybin mushrooms 0.82, DMT 0.82; Datura species (21st in the zoomed panel) 0.72; betel nut (lowest) about 0.08. Mean over 5 to 145 singular values (Fig. 7C, editors' measurement of bar tops at 600 dpi, approximate): ketamine 0.64, LSD 0.61, psilocybin mushrooms 0.60, S. divinorum 0.59, cannabis 0.59; L. williamsii 18th. Ketamine first in about 79% of the settings, LSD about 13%, ibogaine about 6%, L. williamsii about 1% and PCP under 1% (Fig. 7D; editors' measurement of the slice angles, approximate; no shares printed). After deleting the 500 most relevant terms of each of two context topics (20 singular values): top ten ketamine, ayahuasca, S. divinorum, L. williamsii, 5-MeO-DMT, LSD, cannabis, psilocybin mushrooms, iboga, nitrous oxide. By class (Fig. 4): dissociatives first, then deliriants and serotonergic psychedelics; dissociatives differed from every class except deliriants (pairwise tests at p < 0.05, 12 of 21 pairs marked significant, editors' count; no correction reported). NDE subsets: ketamine first in almost all; LSD comparable after cardiac arrest.
claim.rating_reasoning: Observational evidence (a cross-sectional text analysis of two existing collections of written reports) starts low; rated down two levels for risk of bias and one for imprecision, it is very low, the floor. Rated as worded: an association between the substance a report names and how closely its pooled word use resembles pooled near-death accounts, in these two self-selected collections. The claim does not say that ketamine produces an experience like a near-death experience, that near-death experiences have a ketamine-like chemical cause, or that ketamine is a safe experimental model: the abstract's and conclusion's statements to that effect are not adopted, because safety was not studied and the discussion itself says the analysis neither validates nor refutes neurochemical models (p. 65). What the design cannot show is said in the statement: word co-occurrence is not experience, the near-death accounts were written about two decades after the events and some followed anaesthesia or drug use, and nothing about the Erowid writers or their doses is known. 'Is associated with' because the design is observational and the certainty very low (METHODS §6.1). Values are the editors' readings of figures that print none, labelled as approximate. Status single study.

questions_now.q: Across all MDMA therapy trials, which side effects were common?

lines_now.short: In trials, MDMA often caused side effects such as a tight jaw, worry, less appetite or feeling sick, mostly gone within a week.
lines_now.but: Many trials only noted problems people mentioned themselves, some recorded problems were left out of the published papers, and there is too little information on what happens later.
how: These effects were more common than with a dummy pill or a very small dose.
In one small trial in people with a serious illness, 11 of 13 on MDMA had a tight jaw, against 1 of 5 on a dummy pill.
One review found one serious problem linked to MDMA: extra heartbeats the person already had became more frequent and needed a night of monitoring in hospital.
Of the problems listed in trial records, more than half of the minor ones and 4 serious ones, all in people on MDMA, never made it into the published papers.
lines_now.rate: Reviews pooling 8 trials with 298 people, mostly PTSD trials from one sponsor. Staff noting side effects probably knew who got MDMA, and few trials looked beyond PTSD.

claim.statement: In the clinical trials of MDMA-assisted therapy reviewed up to 2024, almost all in PTSD (outside PTSD, one randomized trial each in 12 autistic adults with social anxiety and in 18 people with anxiety related to a life-threatening illness, plus small open-label studies and a case series), MDMA compared with placebo or low-dose MDMA increased common side effects during sessions and in the following week, such as jaw clenching or muscle tightness, anxiety, reduced appetite, nausea, sweating, feeling cold and headache, which the reviews describe as mostly mild to moderate and largely transient. A 2024 meta-analysis found higher odds of any expected reaction during sessions in phase 2 trials (odds ratio 1.67, 95% CI 1.12 to 2.49) and of any treatment-emergent adverse event in the two phase 3 trials (3.51, 2.76 to 4.46), although its any-event percentages cannot be shares of participants; in the life-threatening-illness trial, jaw clenching occurred in 11 of 13 people on MDMA and 1 of 5 on placebo. The meta-analysis found no difference in psychiatric adverse events (phase 2), in suicidality or cardiac events of special interest (phase 3) or in dropping out, and a network meta-analysis found no excess of severe adverse events; a 2022 review found one serious adverse event related to MDMA in the studies it covered (more frequent premature heartbeats, present before treatment, needing a night of hospital monitoring). The record of harms is weak: most studies relied on spontaneous reports, no trial reported harms adequately by the CONSORT Harms 2022 standard, 56% of the non-serious and 4 of the 13 serious adverse events listed in the trial registries were missing from the publications (the 4 all in MDMA groups), and the meta-analysis found too little data on risks beyond active treatment, from small and highly selected samples. Certainty: low (for the increase in common side effects). Status: replicated by the same team.
claim.population: People treated in clinical trials of MDMA-assisted therapy: mostly adults with PTSD; also autistic adults with social anxiety, people with anxiety related to a life-threatening illness, people with alcohol use disorder (open-label) and couples in which one partner has PTSD
claim.exposure: MDMA in one to three sessions within psychotherapy
claim.comparator: Inactive placebo or low-dose MDMA with the same psychotherapy
claim.outcome: Side effects and adverse events during and after treatment, serious adverse events, adverse events of special interest, withdrawal, and completeness of harms reporting
claim.magnitude: Colcott 2024 (8 randomized trials, 298 participants, in the meta-analyses; 13 studies, 333 participants, in the review): phase 2, any expected reaction during sessions OR 1.67 (1.12 to 2.49), 45% against 30%; in the following 7 days OR 1.59 (1.12 to 2.24), 46% against 31%; anxiety OR 4.84 and jaw clenching OR 4.72 during sessions (Fig. 2; the Discussion prints the two the other way round); phase 3, any TEAE OR 3.51 (2.76 to 4.46), 16% against 5% (unit unclear), 13 named TEAEs more frequent; no difference in phase 2 TEAEs or psychiatric TEAEs, phase 3 suicidality or cardiac AESIs, or withdrawal. Registers against publications: 1487 against 661 non-serious events (5 trials), 13 against 9 serious events (8 trials). Life-threatening illness trial (Schipper 2024, Table 4): jaw clenching 11/13 (84.6%) against 1/5 (20.0%), thirst 11/13 against 2/5, perspiration 9/13 against 0/5; no treatment-related serious adverse events. Autistic adults (Breeksema 2022, Table 1): acute anxiety 6/8 against 1/4.
claim.rating_reasoning: Randomized comparisons start high. Rated down once for risk of bias (spontaneous, probably unblinded recording) and once for indirectness (a claim across indications resting mostly on PTSD trials of one sponsor, seen through systematic reviews). Certainty applies to the increase in common side effects; rare, serious or delayed harms cannot be assessed from these trials, which the claim says. The causal verb is used because the comparisons are randomized and the effects are those expected pharmacologically, although the reviews themselves describe them as associations. Most trials share the sponsor and protocol, hence replicated by the same team. This overlaps the phase 3 adverse-event claim in this section, which rests on the trial reports read directly.

questions_now.q: Why can the usual amount be dangerous after a break?

lines_now.short: Two reviews say tolerance to opioids may fall after a break from using them.
lines_now.but: The reviews give no numbers: not how long a break must be, nor how much risk changes.
how: After a break, a dose that used to feel usual might have a much stronger effect, including on breathing.
The main study behind this idea looked at hair samples from people who died of heroin overdose.
One review gives prison and detox as examples of a break. The review it cites does not.
Two studies of people on methadone found tolerance to its effect on breathing was not complete.
lines_now.rate: Two reviews, one citing the other, describing a few older studies. The original studies couldn't be checked, and the key one, the review itself says, only hints at this.

claim.statement: As described second-hand by two narrative reviews (no primary study of this was read), tolerance to opioids is thought to fall during a period without them, so that a dose that was once usual may have a much greater effect, including on breathing, when use starts again. Neither review gives an estimate, so the evidence is insufficient to say how long a break must last, how fast tolerance falls, or by how much the chance of a fatal overdose rises. White and Irvine (1999) offer the idea as a possible explanation and rest it on one hair-analysis study (less morphine in the hair of people who died of heroin overdose than in the hair of people who were still using, which they read as a sign of lower use before death); they say that information on the rate of loss is sparse and that the loss may be quick and uneven between effects, and they describe two studies in people on methadone maintenance that found tolerance to the breathing-depressing effect of methadone to be incomplete. Hickman et al. (2008) say, citing White and Irvine, that risk appears to be raised after periods of relative abstinence, for example following incarceration or detoxification; White and Irvine write of a period of abstinence, and separately of treatment with naltrexone, and do not name either of those settings.
claim.population: People who use opioids (heroin, methadone and other opioids), as described in two narrative reviews; no primary study of a break from opioids was read
claim.exposure: A period without opioids (a period of abstinence in the reviews' wording) before use starts again
claim.comparator: Continued regular use; the same person's tolerance before the break
claim.outcome: Tolerance to opioid effects, including breathing depression, and the chance of a fatal overdose when use starts again
claim.magnitude: No estimate in either source. White and Irvine (1999), second-hand: one hair-analysis study (Tagliaro et al., 1998) found lower morphine content in the hair of people who died of heroin overdose than in the hair of people who were still using (no numbers given in the review); the rate of loss of tolerance for euphoric, analgesic and respiratory effects is called sparse, probably uneven and possibly quick (receptor changes can occur in minutes or hours); incomplete tolerance to the breathing-depressing effect of methadone in two studies of people on methadone maintenance (Marks and Goldring, 1973; Santiago et al., 1977; no numbers given). Hickman et al. (2008): risk appears to be raised after periods of relative abstinence; no figures.
claim.rating_reasoning: A claim seen only through reviews starts from the design of the primary studies they describe, here observational (a hair-analysis comparison of people who died of overdose with people who were still using) and human studies of methadone, so it starts low, and is downgraded for risk of bias (primary studies not appraisable) and for indirectness (second-hand; one review cites the other). Certainty very low. The relation is insufficient evidence because neither source gives a size, a time course or a risk figure. Because every supporting anchor is a narrative review, the claim stays at draft and says so in its statement (METHODS 6.3). Status: single study in effect (Hickman et al. rest on White and Irvine for this point). The claim keeps to what the text says: White and Irvine name only a period of abstinence, and the examples of incarceration and detoxification belong to Hickman et al.

questions_now.q: Does music change how a ketamine treatment session goes?

lines_now.short: In one small trial, the top blood pressure number rose less with music.
lines_now.but: Just 32 patients in hospital; the report gave no results on how the sessions felt.
how: 32 patients with hard-to-treat depression had a course of up to six ketamine drips in hospital. Some were picked at random to hear music during each drip; the rest heard none.
With music, the top blood pressure number rose about 7 points less during each drip.
The report we read gives no results on how the sessions felt or whether depression improved.
Earlier, a review found 14 studies of music with ketamine, mostly with other medicines during surgery or tests. It found no study comparing music with no music in ketamine treatment for depression.
lines_now.rate: One trial of 32 patients, which measured only blood pressure, not how sessions felt. Other studies are small, mostly during medical procedures, often in children, and known only through a review.

claim.statement: Evidence is insufficient to say whether music changes how a ketamine or esketamine session feels or how well the treatment works; one randomized trial found a smaller rise in blood pressure with music. In that trial (Greenway et al., 2024; Montreal, 2021 to 2022; registered), 32 patients with treatment-resistant unipolar or bipolar depression, accepted for a clinical course of six intravenous ketamine infusions over 4 weeks (treatment conditions), were randomly assigned to curated music throughout each 40-minute infusion (15) or to usual care without music (17). Across 181 infusions, systolic blood pressure rose from the start to the end of each infusion by 7.4 mm Hg less with music than without (95% CI 2.9 to 12.0; a mean rise of roughly 11.5 against 18.5 mm Hg, read from the figure), while diastolic pressure did not differ detectably (0.8 mm Hg less; the printed interval, −1.59 to 3.18, appears to have its signs transposed); no serious adverse events were recorded. The letter reports nothing on how the sessions felt, dissociation or depression (it says that its secondary outcomes, which it does not name, will be published elsewhere), nor how many patients in each group needed treatment for raised blood pressure (citing an expert review, the authors say that up to 20% of patients given intravenous ketamine for treatment-resistant depression need such treatment); the comparison was with no music, without a sound or attention control, so the music cannot be separated from attention or expectation; and one patient given usual care was left out of the analysis without a stated reason. Before that trial, as described in one scoping review (Kheirkhah et al., 2024; searched to December 2023; the included studies were not appraised, so its figures are second-hand), 14 studies of music with ketamine had been published, all in patients in clinical or trial settings. In nine, ketamine was given with other sedatives or painkillers, during procedures or, in one study, air medical transport; in most of them music went with less sedation or drug use and lower anxiety, pain or fear, but one trial found no effect on emergence reactions and another found more dreams or emergence reactions with music, though no unpleasant dreams, against 10 controls with unpleasant dreams. Of the five studies of ketamine or esketamine alone, only one compared people who listened with people who heard nothing: in 46 children having heart catheterization under ketamine anaesthesia, the 23 who heard recordings of their mothers' voices (musical in 12 of them) had less anxiety before the procedure and fewer emergence reactions than 23 who wore headphones with no recording. The other four were case reports and interview studies without such a comparison: a woman on esketamine nasal spray found that music of her choice helped with dissociation, confusion and anxiety; two patients with bipolar depression tolerated dissociation better with preferred music in later infusions, which may reflect getting used to the infusions; in 12 people given ketamine in a trial for alcohol use disorder, everyone who listened to music heard it distorted in speed and pitch, felt as good or bad depending on their state; and in 17 people on oral esketamine for depression, music was described as blocking distractions and helping inner exploration, but some felt it kept them tied to the outside world and one stopped using it. Up to its search, the review found no study comparing music with no music during ketamine or esketamine treatment for depression, and its own limitations say no conclusions can be drawn. Certainty: very low. Status: single study.
claim.population: 32 patients with treatment-resistant unipolar or bipolar depression receiving a clinical course of intravenous ketamine in Montreal (one randomized trial), and patients given ketamine or esketamine in clinical settings (anaesthesia, sedation, depression and alcohol-use-disorder treatment) in 14 earlier studies gathered by a scoping review
claim.exposure: Curated music throughout each 40-minute ketamine infusion (trial); music (or, in one study, recordings of mothers' voices) before, during or after ketamine or esketamine (review)
claim.comparator: Usual care without music (trial); no music (headphones with no recording, or a blank soundtrack) in most procedural trials and in the one comparison of ketamine alone; no comparison in the case reports and interview studies (review)
claim.outcome: Rise in systolic and diastolic blood pressure from the start to the end of each infusion (trial); anxiety, pain, emergence reactions, sedative use, dissociation and how the session was experienced (review)
claim.magnitude: Greenway et al. (2024), randomized, 181 infusions in 32 patients (31 apparently analysed for the primary outcome, editors' inference from the flow diagram): change in systolic blood pressure from 0 to 40 minutes, music against no music, β −7.4 mm Hg (95% CI −12.0 to −2.9), P = .008; diastolic β −0.8 mm Hg (printed 95% CI −1.59 to 3.18, an interval centred on +0.8, so its signs appear transposed), P = .58; read approximately from the figure, mean systolic rise about 11.5 mm Hg with music and 18.5 mm Hg without; no clinical, experience or depression outcome reported. Kheirkhah et al. (2024): no pooled estimates. 14 studies: 9 with other sedatives (music with less sedation and lower anxiety or pain in most; no effect on emergence reactions in one; more dreams or emergence reactions in another); 5 with ketamine or esketamine alone, one comparing listeners with children who heard nothing (46 children: mothers' voices against headphones with no recording), the rest case reports (3 patients) and interview studies (17 and 12 people). No study comparing music with no music during ketamine treatment for depression up to December 2023.
claim.rating_reasoning: The best evidence is now one randomized trial, which starts high, but it answers only blood pressure: on its own, the smaller systolic rise with music would rate low (high, minus one for risk of bias and one for imprecision). For how a session feels, the evidence is still the review's small, mostly procedural studies seen second-hand (low, minus risk of bias and indirectness, giving very low). Rated for the claim as worded: down one each for risk of bias, indirectness and imprecision, giving very low. Status single study: one randomized trial for blood pressure, and, for ketamine or esketamine alone, one comparison of listening with not listening (46 children under anaesthesia hearing recordings of their mothers' voices), seen through one review. The claim no longer rests only on a narrative review (METHODS §6.3), and every anchor has been checked by a second reader. The trial's secondary outcomes, deferred to later publications, have not been seen.

questions_now.q: How often do people seek emergency treatment after LSD?
How often do people seek emergency treatment after LSD?

lines_now.short: About 10 in 1,000 people who had used LSD in the past year said they sought emergency treatment, in one big online survey. After magic mushrooms: 2 in 1,000.
lines_now.but: Volunteers answered an online survey about themselves; nobody checked their answers, or whether the drug was really LSD.
how: In the 2017 Global Drug Survey, 10,293 people who had used LSD in the past year answered this question; 102 said yes.
Most of the 102 had panic, anxiety or confusion; 21 reported thoughts or acts of self-harm, and about half said they were admitted to hospital.
Of about 98 who said how long it lasted, 58 felt back to normal within a day; 11 still had problems after 4 weeks.
People with a past mental health diagnosis reported seeking emergency treatment more often: 1.8 in 100, against 0.7 in 100.
lines_now.rate: One online survey of volunteers in 2016–17, who reported on themselves. Nobody checked hospital records or whether the drug was really LSD, and people who could not answer are missing.

freq.what: people who had used LSD in the past year said they sought emergency treatment afterwards
freq.note: Global Drug Survey 2017, online volunteers: 102 of 10,293 for LSD and 19 of 9,233 for magic mushrooms, all self-reported.

claim.statement: In people who had used LSD in the past 12 months and took part in the Global Drug Survey 2017, an anonymous online survey of drug use open from November 2016 to January 2017 in 10 languages, which people chose to join through social networks, media partners and harm-reduction organisations and were not paid for (13,769 respondents reported past-year use: 63.9% were under 25, 79.6% men, and most lived in Germany, the USA, the UK, Denmark, Canada or Australia), 102 of the 10,293 who answered the question (1.0%; about 1 in 100, or 10 in 1,000) said they had sought emergency medical treatment after LSD in that year (Kopra, Ferris, Rucker, et al., 2022). The denominator is the people who answered that question (75% of those reporting past-year use, editors' calculation), not everyone who reported past-year use, although the abstract describes the 10,293 as the past-year group. Emergency treatment was not defined, answers were not checked against any record, nothing that was taken was tested, and the number of incidents per person was not asked; dividing the 102 people by an estimated 53,627 days of use (a mean of 5.21 days a year), the authors put the figure at 0.2% of past-year uses, which they call an underestimate because each person is counted once. In the companion analysis of the same survey, 19 of 9,233 people who had used magic mushrooms in the past year and answered (0.2%; about 2 in 1,000) said they had sought emergency treatment after them, a share the authors describe as about five times lower (Kopra, Ferris, Winstock, et al., 2022). Saying yes was more common among people with a lifetime mental health diagnosis (1.8% against 0.7%; χ2(1, N = 8,299) = 19.33, p < 0.001), among younger people (median age 21 against 22; p = 0.003) and among those with more days of use in the past year (median 3 against 2; p = 0.029), in separate tests without adjustment, and it did not differ by sex or by first use in the past year. Of the 102, most ticked anxiety or panic (71) and confusion (66), and many paranoia (50) or seeing or hearing things (46); 21 (20.6%) ticked thoughts or acts of self-harm, 17 (16.7%) an accident or trauma, 13 (12.7%) seizures and 12 (11.8%) passing out, none of it verified, and the authors say it is unknown which symptoms came from LSD and which from other drugs taken. 54.5% said they had been admitted to hospital, a share the authors call surprising and print without a count, noting that the survey did not define admission. The paper gives recovery as percentages without a denominator, 59.2% back to normal within 24 hours and 11.2% with consequences lasting beyond 4 weeks; both fit 98 respondents, and the editors' reading of the figure, which prints no values, gives 58 of 98 back to normal within 24 hours, 40 taking longer, 17 not back to normal after 5 to 7 days and 11 with problems beyond 4 weeks, 6 of whom said they had not recovered (the abstract gives the 11). In the session that led to emergency treatment, 33 of the 102 had taken nothing else and 69 (editors' subtraction) had also taken another substance, most often cannabis (51) or alcohol (24); how often people combined substances in sessions that did not end in emergency treatment was not asked. Choosing up to three of six reasons, 53.9% named the setting, 50.0% their mindset, 40.2% taking too much and 34.3% mixing with other drugs; about 13 of the 102 thought the drug had not been LSD and about 10 did not know (both read by the editors from a figure that prints no values). Afterwards, 62.7% said they had cut down their LSD use and 16.7% that it had not changed. The authors cite similar shares in later rounds of the same survey (0.9%, 1.0% and 0.8% in the 2019, 2020 and 2021 rounds; those reports were not read here); they write that the incidents captured are likely only a proportion of LSD-related adverse events, most likely the more severe ones, that some serious reactions may not lead to emergency treatment (for example from fear of legal consequences), that some visits may be false alarms raised by others, and that drugs mistaken for LSD, such as NBOMes, may account for some incidents. They read their results as showing LSD to be relatively safe when used recreationally, with adverse reactions 'typically short-lived, self-limiting and psychological in nature', while their own figures show 40 of 98 taking longer than a day and 21 of 102 reporting thoughts or acts of self-harm; the survey cannot count deaths or people who could not or did not answer. The survey's founder and owner is an author; King's College London receives funding from COMPASS Pathways for psilocybin trials led by two of the authors, one of whom (Rucker) has been paid as a consultant by Clerkenwell Health and Beckley PsyTech, and the other (Young) has had honoraria and consulting fees from several drug companies and co-edits the publishing journal; the funding statement names UK National Institute for Health Research support for those two authors and no funder for the survey. Certainty: very low. Status: single study.
claim.population: Respondents to the Global Drug Survey 2017 (anonymous, online, self-nominated; November 2016 to January 2017; 10 languages) who reported LSD use in the past 12 months (13,769; 63.9% under 25, 79.6% men, most living in Germany, the USA, the UK, Denmark, Canada or Australia), of whom 10,293 answered the emergency-treatment question
claim.exposure: Use of LSD in the past 12 months, self-reported; nothing tested, so what was taken is not confirmed; other substances in the incident session as reported
claim.comparator: None outside the sample: within it, respondents who answered and did not report seeking emergency treatment (for age, sex, mental health diagnosis, first use, doses per day of use and frequency of use); in the companion analysis of the same survey, respondents who had used magic mushrooms
claim.outcome: Self-reported seeking of emergency medical treatment (not defined) after LSD in the past 12 months; for those who said yes, symptoms ticked from a list of 20, self-reported hospital admission (not defined), time to feel back to normal, other substances in that session, perceived reasons and change in use
claim.magnitude: Kopra, Ferris, Rucker, et al. (2022): 102 of 10,293 who answered (1.0%; editors' Wilson 95% interval 0.82% to 1.20%); per day of use 0.001902 (0.2%; 102 divided by an estimated 53,627 days; an underestimate by the authors' account). Lifetime mental health diagnosis 1.8% against 0.7% (χ2(1, N = 8,299) = 19.33, p < 0.001); median age 21 against 22 (p = 0.003); median days of use 3 against 2 (p = 0.029). Of the 102: anxiety or panic 71, confusion 66, paranoia 50, seeing or hearing things 46, thoughts or acts of self-harm 21 (20.6%), accident or trauma 17 (16.7%), seizures 13 (12.7%), passing out 12 (11.8%); hospital admission 54.5% (no count; not defined); back to normal within 24 hours 59.2% and consequences beyond 4 weeks 11.2% (58 and 11 of 98 by the editors' reading; 40 of 98 longer than 24 hours, 17 longer than 5 to 7 days, 6 not recovered); nothing else taken 33, cannabis 51, alcohol 24; reasons setting 53.9%, mindset 50.0%, too much 40.2%, mixing 34.3%, not LSD about 13 of 102 and don't know about 10 (figure, editors' reading). Companion magic mushroom analysis (Kopra, Ferris, Winstock, et al., 2022): 19 of 9,233 (0.2%), about five times lower by the authors' account.
claim.rating_reasoning: A descriptive claim, rated as a description of the population sampled (METHODS §6.3): starts low; down one for measurement (risk of bias) and one for coverage (indirectness), giving very low, the floor; never upgraded. 'Describes' because it reports how many respondents said they had sought emergency treatment, not a risk for people who use LSD and not a cause of the symptoms. The associations with mental health diagnosis, age and frequency are univariate and are reported as associations among respondents. The question is worded with 'seek', not 'need', because the survey asked whether people had sought emergency treatment, not whether they needed it, and the authors themselves say that some who needed treatment may not have sought it while some visits may have been false alarms. Status single study: one survey wave; the later rounds the authors cite come from the same survey programme and team and were not read, and the magic mushroom figure is a companion analysis of the same survey, so neither counts as replication. The authors' conclusion that reactions are typically short-lived and self-limiting is not adopted, because their own recovery and symptom figures qualify it. Numbers of doses are left out, and 'taking too much' appears only as a reason respondents chose.

questions_now.q: Can other people's cannabis smoke make you fail a urine drug test?
Can other people's cannabis smoke make you fail a urine drug test?

lines_now.short: Rarely at the US government's workplace limit: after an hour in thick cannabis smoke, 1 of 18 people who didn't smoke went over it. At a lower limit, 12 did.
lines_now.but: One small lab test with thick smoke in a sealed room; everyday smoke was not tested.
how: In a sealed room about 3 by 4 metres, 6 people smoked cannabis freely for an hour. 6 people who didn't smoke sat between them.
Only 1 of 250 urine samples went over the US government's workplace limit. It did so on just 1 of 5 labs' tests.
Some private tests use a lower limit. There, 3 to 7 of the 18 would have had a positive that a lab check confirmed.
A positive is a urine result: a THC breakdown product above a set level. It is not a measure of being high.
lines_now.rate: One lab experiment: 18 people, 6 in each of three settings, sat beside people smoking in a sealed room, in thick smoke in two of them. Everyday exposure was not tested.

claim.statement: In 18 adult volunteers in Baltimore, USA (9 women and 9 men, mean age 28), who had used cannabis at some time but not in the previous 6 months by their own account and whose urine was negative before exposure, one hour seated in alternate seats beside six people smoking cannabis cigarettes as they wished, compared with each volunteer's own urine before exposure (there was no unexposed group), was followed by THCCOOH, a breakdown product the body makes from THC, in every volunteer's urine, but only rarely by a positive test at the US federal workplace cut-offs (Cone et al., 2015). Study conditions: a sealed chamber of 3.05 m by 3.96 m with a 2.13 m ceiling; in Session 1, cigarettes of 5.3% THC and no ventilation (10.3 g smoked in the hour by the six people smoking); in Session 2, 11.3% THC and no ventilation (14.4 g); in Session 3, 11.3% THC with ventilation of 11.2 air changes per hour, which the authors liken to home air-conditioning (16.5 g); a different six volunteers in each session, run in that fixed order at weekly or longer intervals; smoke was heavy in Sessions 1 and 2 and visible but greatly reduced in Session 3, and in Session 1 some of the people smoking stopped early after eye irritation, by their own account. Urine was collected from about 1 hour before to 34 hours after (250 specimens, including the 18 taken before exposure, of 252 scheduled) and tested with screening immunoassays at 20 and 50 ng/mL in five laboratories (one assay, CEDIA, also at 75 and 100 ng/mL) and by GC-MS, the confirmation cut-off being the 15 ng/mL of the SAMHSA Mandatory Guidelines for Federal Workplace Drug Testing Programs, whose screening cut-off is 50 ng/mL. THCCOOH became measurable (0.75 ng/mL or more) in all 18 within 0.25 to 3 hours. No specimen screened positive on the CEDIA assay at 100 or 75 ng/mL. At 50 ng/mL, 1 of 250 specimens screened positive, on one of the five laboratories' assays only (the other four reported it negative): one woman's specimen 4 hours after Session 2, which held 46.3 ng/mL by GC-MS, so that under the federal two-step rule (screen at 50, confirm at 15) 1 of the 18 volunteers would have had a positive with that assay and none with the others (editors' count). At the 20 ng/mL screening cut-off, which the authors say some private non-regulated programmes use, positive specimens in Sessions 1, 2 and 3 numbered 12, 22 and 0 on DRI, 6, 8 and 0 on KIMS, 12, 22 and 1 on EMIT II Plus and 6, 12 and 0 on CEDIA; 12 of the 18 volunteers screened positive at least once on at least one assay (5 of 6, 6 of 6 and 1 of 6 by session), and 3 (with KIMS), 6 (with DRI or CEDIA) or 7 (with EMIT II Plus) of the 18 would have had a screening positive confirmed at 15 ng/mL or more by GC-MS, all of them in the unventilated sessions except one volunteer with EMIT II Plus (editors' counts from Table I). In all, 27 specimens from 7 volunteers reached 15 ng/mL (3, 22 and 2 by session; the paper's 10.8% of 250 counts the 18 specimens taken before exposure, so they are 27 of the 232 taken after it, 11.6%, editors' arithmetic), and peak values per volunteer ranged from 1.3 to 57.5 ng/mL. Screening positives at 20 ng/mL first appeared 1 to 4 hours after exposure and continued for 2 to 22 hours; the latest was in one volunteer's 26-to-30-hour pool (15.6 ng/mL, positive on one assay); in the last pool, 30 to 34 hours after, no specimen screened positive on the four assays tabulated at 20 ng/mL or reached 15 ng/mL, although THCCOOH was still measurable in 12 of the 18. The authors' summary that positives are likely to be rare, limited to the hours immediately after exposure and confined to circumstances where exposure is obvious fits the 50 ng/mL screen, not a 20 ng/mL screen; 'immediately' understates positives that lasted up to 22 hours and one at 26 to 30 hours; and only obvious exposure was studied. A positive here is a urine result, a breakdown product of THC at or above a set level, not a measure of intoxication; this paper reports no measure of effects (blood, oral fluid, hair and effect measures were reserved for other reports). Differences between sessions cannot be put down to potency or ventilation alone, because the sessions ran in a fixed order with different people and Session 1 burned less cannabis. Funding: SAMHSA, which issues the federal guidelines whose cut-offs were tested; NIDA supplied the cannabis and funded one author; two authors are SAMHSA employees in its Division of Workplace Programs and the first author consults for that division. Certainty: very low. Status: single study.
claim.population: 18 adult volunteers in Baltimore, USA (9 women, 9 men; mean age 28, range 20 to 45), recruited through advertisements, flyers and word of mouth and paid, who had used cannabis at some time but not in the previous 6 months by their own account, with urine negative for cannabis and other drugs at screening and admission and no or minimal tobacco use; six per session, each in one session only
claim.exposure: One hour seated in alternate seats beside six people smoking cannabis cigarettes as they wished, in a sealed chamber of 3.05 m by 3.96 m with a 2.13 m ceiling (study conditions): Session 1, cigarettes of 5.3% THC, no ventilation, 10.3 g smoked in all; Session 2, 11.3% THC, no ventilation, 14.4 g; Session 3, 11.3% THC with ventilation of 11.2 air changes per hour, 16.5 g
claim.comparator: Each volunteer's own urine about 1 hour before exposure (all negative by GC-MS and immunoassay); no unexposed group and no placebo condition; the three sessions differ in potency, ventilation, amount smoked, people and week, in a fixed order
claim.outcome: Urinary THCCOOH by GC-MS (confirmation cut-off 15 ng/mL) and screening immunoassay results at 20, 50, 75 and 100 ng/mL in specimens collected for 34 hours after exposure: specimens and volunteers screening positive at each cut-off, and those whose screening positive would be confirmed at 15 ng/mL
claim.magnitude: Cone et al. (2015), 18 volunteers, 250 specimens (18 before exposure, 232 after): screening positives at 100 and 75 ng/mL (CEDIA only), 0 of 250; at 50 ng/mL, 1 of 250 (printed 0.4%; one of five laboratories' assays), 46.3 ng/mL by GC-MS, so 1 of 18 volunteers positive under the federal 50 and 15 ng/mL cut-offs with that assay (Wilson 95% interval 1.0% to 25.8%, editors' calculation) and 0 of 18 with the other assays; at 20 ng/mL, positive specimens in Sessions 1, 2 and 3: DRI 12, 22, 0; KIMS 6, 8, 0; EMIT II Plus 12, 22, 1; CEDIA 6, 12, 0 (34, 14, 35 and 18 of 250 in all, editors' sums); volunteers with at least one 20 ng/mL screening positive on any of the four assays, 12 of 18 (66.7%; 43.7% to 83.7%; 5 of 6, 6 of 6 and 1 of 6 by session; editors' count); volunteers with a 20 ng/mL screening positive confirmed at 15 ng/mL or more: KIMS 3, DRI 6, CEDIA 6, EMIT II Plus 7 of 18 (editors' count); specimens at 15 ng/mL or more, 27 (3, 22 and 2 by session) from 7 of 18 volunteers (38.9%; 20.3% to 61.4%), that is 27 of 232 specimens taken after exposure (11.6%; 8.1% to 16.4%) against the printed 10.8% of 250; peak THCCOOH per volunteer by session, mean (range) 11.2 (1.9 to 20.1), 28.3 (5.5 to 57.5) and 7.5 (1.3 to 15.5) ng/mL; THCCOOH measurable (0.75 ng/mL or more) in 18 of 18 within 0.25 to 3 hours and in 12 of 18 in the 30-to-34-hour pool; latest screening positive in one volunteer's 26-to-30-hour pool (15.6 ng/mL), none in the 30-to-34-hour pools (editors' count). No unexposed group, so no difference from unexposed people can be given.
claim.rating_reasoning: A controlled exposure in volunteers without a placebo or unexposed condition, its three conditions run in a fixed order with different people, does not meet the rule under which within-person laboratory studies start high (placebo-controlled, with randomized or counterbalanced order); what happened to the volunteers' urine is rated as a description of these conditions (METHODS §6.3), starting low. Indirectness −1 (an extreme, obvious exposure in a small sealed room, while the question is about other people's smoke in general) and imprecision −1 (18 volunteers, 6 per condition) bring it to very low, the floor. Not rated down for risk of bias: the urine results are objective, complete and fully tabulated, and the editors' recount from Table I reproduces every printed count; the serious risk of bias of the comparisons between sessions (ROBINS-I; fixed order, different volunteers) is not used, because the claim does not attribute differences to potency or ventilation. Worded as 'describes': the exposure plainly put THCCOOH into urine (every pre-exposure specimen negative, every volunteer measurable within 3 hours), but the claim's point is how many tests would read positive at each cut-off, a count under these conditions. The authors' 'rare' is adopted only for the 50 ng/mL screen, with the counts at 20 ng/mL beside it; 'only where exposure is obvious' is not adopted, because only obvious exposure was studied. The counts of volunteers and of confirmed positives are editors' counts from Table I (minus signs read from the rendered pages and from the PDF's symbol font), to be recomputed by the second reader. Status single study: the authors say earlier passive-exposure studies, mostly with weaker cannabis, also found THC metabolites in non-smokers' urine, but those were not read here. Funding by SAMHSA, which issues the guidelines tested, and the authors' ties to it are given in the statement. Amounts appear only as study conditions, and nothing is phrased as advice about tests.

questions_now.q: Do benzodiazepine strips find the newer benzodiazepines sold on the street?

lines_now.short: Often not. At one drug-checking service, strips missed 9 of 24 samples with newer benzodiazepines.
lines_now.but: A lab checked only some samples. Many were picked because of a suspected overdose.
how: At eight health sites, samples were tested with strips, and a lab checked some of them.
Strips showed newer benzodiazepines in 15 of 24 samples, but in only 8 of 16 with etizolam alone.
They also read positive in 20 of 129 samples in which the lab found none.
In a lab, the same maker's strip never reacted to pure etizolam. An earlier report said similar strips seemed to pick it up in larger amounts, so the two disagree.
lines_now.rate: One brand of urine strip, tried at one Canadian drug-checking programme and on pure samples in a lab. Only 159 of 1368 samples were lab-checked, and those were not picked at random.

freq.what: samples with a newer benzodiazepine showed it on the strip
freq.note: 15 of 24 samples at one drug-checking service, 2018 to 2020. With etizolam alone, 8 of 16.

claim.statement: In drug-checking samples brought to eight harm-reduction sites in Vancouver and Surrey between October 2018 and January 2020, benzodiazepine urine test strips (BTNX Rapid Response, made to detect urine metabolites of common benzodiazepines) read at the sites, after infrared spectroscopy of the same sample and with one combined result recorded, compared with confirmatory laboratory tests on a convenience subset of 153 samples from five of the sites, partly chosen because of suspected benzodiazepine overdose, missed many of the newer benzodiazepines not sold as medicines (NPS benzodiazepines) and also gave false positives. The strips read positive in 15 of 24 samples that contained an NPS benzodiazepine (62.5%; editors' Wilson 95% CI 42.7–78.8%): in 7 of 8 when flualprazolam, flubromazolam or flubromazepam was present, but in 8 of 16 when etizolam was the only one (50%). They also read positive in 20 of 129 samples in which no NPS benzodiazepine was found (15.5%; 10.3–22.7%), and what made those react was not reported. Infrared spectroscopy (FTIR), used beside the strips, found 2 of the 24. The strips detected the prescribed benzodiazepines alprazolam and temazepam in all six samples that held only these (Laing et al., 2021). In pure solutions, the same maker's benzodiazepine strip detected diazepam and alprazolam from 0.1 µg/mL and bromazolam and flubromazepam from 0.25 µg/mL, but did not react to etizolam at any concentration tried from 0.01 to 0.5 mg/mL, 40 times or more the concentrations at which it detected the others (editors' calculation) (Sisco, Appley, et al., 2024). A report relayed second-hand by Laing et al. concluded that newer benzodiazepines appear to be detected by similar strips, etizolam at a higher minimum concentration than other NPS benzodiazepines, still within the range useful for drug checking (Shapiro et al., 2020), so the sources disagree on whether these strips react to etizolam at all; differences in lots or test conditions may explain it, but this was not shown. Only 159 of 1368 strip-tested samples had laboratory confirmation, the two confirmatory laboratories disagreed on 2 of 7 positive samples tested at both, etizolam is reported to dissolve poorly in water, and targeted laboratory methods may miss the newest compounds; none of the 24 samples was expected by the person to contain an NPS benzodiazepine, and 17 of them also contained fentanyl. Certainty: very low. Status: replicated.
claim.population: Drug-checking samples brought to eight harm-reduction sites in Vancouver and Surrey, Canada (2018 to 2020), of which 153 had confirmatory laboratory results; benzodiazepines in water in a second laboratory
claim.exposure: BTNX benzodiazepine urine test strips (oxazepam calibrator, cut-off 300 ng/mL) used on dissolved drug at the sites after FTIR of the same sample, with one combined result recorded; the same maker's strip in pure solutions
claim.comparator: Confirmatory laboratory testing (GC–MS, LC-MS or qNMR) for NPS benzodiazepines; known content of prepared solutions
claim.outcome: Detection of NPS benzodiazepines (sensitivity), false positives, and detection of individual benzodiazepines in water
claim.magnitude: Laing et al. (153 samples with point-of-care and confirmatory results; 6 with only typical benzodiazepines removed): strips 15/24 NPS-benzodiazepine samples positive (62.5%; Wilson 42.7–78.8%, editors' calculation), false-negative rate 37.5%; 20/129 negatives positive (15.5%; 10.3–22.7%), specificity 84.5% (editors' calculation); 87.5% (n = 8) with flualprazolam, flubromazolam or flubromazepam; 50.0% (n = 16; 28.0–72.0%) with etizolam alone; FTIR 2/24 (false-negative rate 91.7%), false-positive rate 3.9%; either method 17/24 detected, 23 false positives. Sisco, Appley, et al. (2024): limits 0.1 µg/mL (diazepam, alprazolam) and 0.25 µg/mL (bromazolam, flubromazepam); etizolam negative from 0.01 to 0.5 mg/mL, 40 to 100 times or more those limits (editors' calculation). Second-hand (Shapiro et al., 2020, via Laing et al.): similar strips appear to detect etizolam at a higher minimum concentration than flualprazolam and flubromazolam.
claim.rating_reasoning: Test-accuracy evidence starts high; Laing et al.'s agreement figures are accuracy evidence with high risk of bias (METHODS §6.3), so two levels for risk of bias and one each for indirectness and imprecision take it to the floor of very low. Rated as worded. Status replicated: independent teams (British Columbia; NIST) both found etizolam poorly detected; Sisco, Appley, et al. (2024) is re-filed as test-accuracy with QUADAS-2 in this round; the Shapiro et al. report is second-hand and not counted.

questions_now.q: Do xylazine test strips work?

lines_now.short: Strips found xylazine in 37 of 38 samples with enough of it, but often missed small amounts.
lines_now.but: One batch of strips was read in a lab. The samples were residues from used equipment, not powders.
how: A lab tested 100 residue samples wiped from used syringes, bags and pill bottles, and checked them with a lab machine.
With enough xylazine, 37 of 38 read positive. With less, only 6 of 28 did. None of 34 without xylazine read positive.
In pure water, every strip read positive only from 2.5 times the amount the strip is made to find.
Lidocaine, a common cutting agent, also made strips positive. At the one amount tested, they did not react to medetomidine. It is a similar drug used on animals.
lines_now.rate: Two lab studies by one team. The main figure leaves out samples with only a little xylazine, and the study doesn't say how samples were chosen or whether strip readers knew the right answers.

freq.title: Out of every 100 samples with xylazine, how many read positive?
pairs: samples with at least the amount the strip is made to find
freq.note: 37 of 38 and 6 of 28 residue samples, one batch of strips, read in a lab.

claim.statement: In residue samples swabbed from used drug equipment and in pure xylazine solutions, one production lot of BTNX xylazine test strips read in a laboratory, compared with quantitative GC-MS/MS or known content, read positive in nearly all residue samples with at least the strip's listed amount of xylazine, read positive on every strip in pure solutions only from 2.5 times that amount, and often missed smaller amounts. Of 100 residue samples from syringes, bags and pill bottles collected in two US states, the strips read positive in 37 of 38 with xylazine at or above the listed 1 µg/mL cut-off (sensitivity 97.4%; editors' Wilson 95% CI 86.5–99.5%; the one miss had 2 µg/mL) and in none of 34 without xylazine (one faint; specificity 100%; 89.8–100%), but in only 6 of 28 with less xylazine, so 43 of all 66 xylazine-containing samples read positive (65%; 53–76%; editors' calculation). In pure solutions, all 15 strips per level read positive from 2.5 µg/mL; at the listed 1 µg/mL cut-off 3 of 15 were positive and 12 showed a faint test band, counted as negative. Of 76 other compounds tested at 100 µg/mL with two strips each, only lidocaine, a common cutting agent, read positive; the veterinary sedative medetomidine and the α2-agonists clonidine, detomidine, romifidine and tizanidine did not at that concentration, the only one tested, so at that level these strips would not show them; higher concentrations, as from dissolved powders, were not tested (Sisco, Nestadt, et al., 2024). A later version of the strip with a different antibody, tested in water in the same first author's laboratory, detected 1 µg/mL, did not react to lidocaine, levamisole, ketamine or medetomidine, reacted to brimonidine, clonidine, romifidine and tizanidine at high concentrations, and after two weeks unopened at 55 °C needed 10 µg/mL (Sisco, Appley, et al., 2024). Powders and pills dissolved as people do, other lots and brands, and reading outside a laboratory were not tested. Certainty: low. Status: replicated by the same team.
claim.population: 100 drug residue samples swabbed from used drug equipment in two US states, and pure xylazine and 76 other compounds in water
claim.exposure: One production lot of BTNX xylazine test strips, two strips per sample, read in a laboratory; a later version with a different antibody in a second study
claim.comparator: GC-MS/MS quantitation of xylazine in each residue sample; known content of prepared solutions
claim.outcome: Sensitivity and specificity on residue samples, the lowest concentration giving consistent positives, and reactions to other compounds
claim.magnitude: Sisco, Nestadt, et al. (2024), residues: 1 µg/mL or more 37/38 positive (97.4%; Wilson 86.5–99.5%; the one miss at 2 µg/mL); none detected 0/34 positive, 1 faint (specificity 100%; 89.8–100%); below 1 µg/mL 6/28 positive, 10 faint, 12 negative; all xylazine-containing samples 43/66 positive (65%; 53–76%) (editors' calculations on the card). Pure xylazine: 15/15 positive at 2.5 µg/mL and above; 3/15 at 1 µg/mL (12 faint); 7/15 at 0.5 µg/mL (8 faint); 0/15 at 0.1 µg/mL. Cross-reactivity at 100 µg/mL only: lidocaine alone of 76 other compounds. Sisco, Appley, et al. (2024), newer version: limit 1 µg/mL; brimonidine, clonidine, romifidine and tizanidine cross-reacted at high concentrations; heated strips needed 10 µg/mL.

questions_now.q: What else has MDMA therapy been tried for?

lines_now.short: Outside PTSD, nobody can yet say whether MDMA therapy helps.
lines_now.but: Each condition had at most one very small trial, and people could usually tell whether they had MDMA.
how: Reviews up to 2024 found single small trials in people anxious about a serious illness, autistic adults with social anxiety, and people with tinnitus.
Studies in people with alcohol problems and in couples had no comparison group.
In the serious-illness trial, anxiety fell more with MDMA, but the trial was too small to be sure.
A critical review found that only the two later PTSD trials met its basic standard.
lines_now.rate: Outside PTSD, each condition has had one small trial at most, the largest with 18 people. People could usually tell whether they had MDMA and rated their own symptoms.

claim.statement: For conditions other than PTSD, evidence is insufficient to say whether MDMA-assisted therapy helps. The systematic reviews read here (searches up to March 2024) found only small studies outside PTSD: one randomized trial each in anxiety related to a life-threatening illness (18 people), social anxiety in autistic adults (12) and tinnitus (13), an open-label study in alcohol use disorder (14), an uncontrolled study of couples in which one partner has PTSD (6 couples) and a Swiss case series. The Cochrane review rated the evidence in life-threatening illness very uncertain: in its one trial, MDMA against placebo changed trait anxiety by −14.7 points on a 20 to 80 scale (95% CI −29.45 to 0.05) and depression by −6.3 points on a 0 to 63 scale (−16.93 to 4.33). A network meta-analysis of depressive symptoms, whose MDMA trials were mostly in PTSD, found high-dose MDMA better than the placebo arms of psychedelic trials by 5.3 HAMD-17 points (95% credible interval 2.26 to 8.32) but not clearly better than the placebo arms of antidepressant trials (1.5, −2.79 to 5.78), a comparison made only indirectly. A critical narrative review found that, for MDMA, only the two phase 3 PTSD trials met its minimum standard (randomized, more than 15 people per group) and called MDMA for PTSD a signal needing replication. The reviews report that blinding was rarely achieved and that controlled follow-up was short. Certainty: very low. Status: single study (one trial per condition outside PTSD).
claim.population: People with conditions other than PTSD: anxiety related to a life-threatening illness, social anxiety in autistic adults, tinnitus, alcohol use disorder, couples with one partner with PTSD, depressive symptoms

claim.comparator: Placebo or low-dose MDMA with the same therapy; none in open-label and uncontrolled studies
claim.outcome: Condition-specific symptoms (anxiety, depression); number and design of the trials available
claim.magnitude: Life-threatening illness (Cochrane, 1 trial, 18): STAI-T −14.70 (95% CI −29.45 to 0.05), STAI-S −16.10 (−33.03 to 0.83), BDI-II −6.30 (−16.93 to 4.33), very low certainty. Depressive symptoms (network meta-analysis; MDMA trials mostly PTSD): high-dose MDMA against psychedelic-trial placebo 5.32 HAMD-17 points (2.26 to 8.32); against antidepressant-trial placebo 1.53 (−2.79 to 5.78). Starting from randomized trials, rated down once for risk of bias (unblinding) and twice for imprecision, giving very low certainty, which matches the Cochrane rating for MDMA. questions_now.q: Can psilocybin help people drink less?
Can psilocybin help people drink less?

lines_now.short: Maybe. In one trial, people given psilocybin with talk therapy drank heavily on about 10 in 100 days, against 24 with a comparison pill.
lines_now.but: Almost everyone could tell if they got psilocybin, and people reported their own drinking.
how: At 2 US universities, 93 adults dependent on alcohol were offered 12 talk-therapy sessions. Chance decided who also got psilocybin twice or a comparison pill.
Heavy drinking had already more than halved in both groups during 4 weeks of therapy. That was before any psilocybin or comparison pill.
After about 94 in 100 sessions, people guessed right whether they had psilocybin. So what they expected may explain part of the gap.
lines_now.rate: One trial of 93 adults with drinking problems: almost everyone could tell whether they got psilocybin, and they reported their own drinking. It was too small to be sure how big the difference is.

freq.title: Out of every 100 days in the 8 months after the first dose, how many were heavy-drinking days?
pairs: days for people given psilocybin with talk therapy
days for people given a comparison pill with the same therapy
freq.note: One trial of 93 adults with alcohol use disorder at two US universities: 9.7 against 23.6 in 100 days, as people reported them. Heavy drinking had more than halved in both groups before any pill.

claim.statement: In adults with DSM-IV alcohol dependence who were not in treatment and had no major psychiatric or other drug use disorder, recruited through local media at two US academic centres (University of New Mexico, 2014 to 2015; New York University, 2015 to 2020) (Bogenschutz et al., 2022; 95 randomized, 93 treated and analysed; mean age 46; 42 of 95 women; 75 of 95 non-Hispanic White; median household income $100 000; in the 12 weeks before screening, drinking on 74.9% of days and heavily on 52.7%), psilocybin given by clinicians in two 8-hour sessions within 12 sessions of psychotherapy (motivational interviewing and cognitive behavioural therapy from a team of two therapists including a psychiatrist; trial conditions: 25 mg/70 kg by mouth at week 4, then 30 or 40 mg/70 kg at week 8), compared with diphenhydramine (an antihistamine) as an active placebo with the same psychotherapy (50 mg, then 100 mg), is associated with fewer self-reported heavy drinking days (5 or more drinks in a day for men, 4 or more for women) over the 32 weeks (8 months) after the first dose: 9.71% of days with psilocybin (48 people) against 23.57% with diphenhydramine (45), a difference of 13.86 percentage points (95% CI 3.00 to 24.72; Hedges g 0.52, 0.11 to 0.94), so that heavy drinking days in the psilocybin group were 41% of those in the diphenhydramine group. The Methods give the prespecified primary window as weeks 5 to 32, while the abstract, results, tables and figure use weeks 5 to 36, the 32-week double-blind period; the registry record and protocol were not read. Both groups had already cut heavy drinking sharply before any medication, during 4 weeks of psychotherapy while trying to stop drinking: from 56.48% to 24.11% of days in those later given psilocybin and from 48.57% to 21.31% in those later given diphenhydramine (decreases of 32.37 points, 95% CI 23.68 to 41.07, and 27.26, 20.83 to 33.69), so both groups more than halved their heavy drinking days before the first dose, about two-thirds of the psilocybin group's fall from screening to the follow-up mean came before it, and the diphenhydramine group's follow-up mean was close to its level in the 4 weeks before dosing (editors' arithmetic; the paper does not say whether its follow-up means are observed or model estimates). Participants guessed their medication correctly after 93.6% of first and 94.7% of second medication sessions, and therapists after 92.4% and 97.4% (percentages without the numbers of guesses); the authors name the failure of diphenhydramine to keep the blind as their first limitation and say biased expectancies could have influenced the results. Drinking was reported by the participants in timeline follow-back interviews; a hair or fingernail alcohol marker (EtG) at week 24 was available for 50 of 93 and was negative in all 14 who reported total abstinence. Exploratory secondary outcomes, without correction for multiple comparisons: drinks per day 1.17 against 2.26 (difference 1.09, 0.27 to 1.92); no heavy drinking days at all in the 32 weeks, 16 of 48 against 5 of 45 (odds ratio 4, 1.32 to 12.10); no drinking at all, 11 of 48 against 4 of 45 (odds ratio 3.05, 0.89 to 10.40); in the final month, no drinking 23 of 48 against 11 of 45. There were no serious adverse events with psilocybin and three, all during binge drinking, with diphenhydramine; within 48 hours of dosing, headache occurred in 21 of 48 against 2 of 45, and two people given psilocybin received a sedative for anxiety during their second session. Enrolment stopped at 95 of up to 180 planned when COVID-19 halted recruitment; the authors state that participants drank less intensely at screening than in most medication trials for alcohol use disorder, that the two-group design cannot separate the effect of the psychotherapy, and that effects beyond 32 weeks are unknown. Funding: the Heffter Research Institute, which reviewed and approved the protocol, an NIH translational-science grant and individual donors; the first author is named as inventor on a provisional patent application related to this work filed by his employer, with his rights waived, the employer licensed commercial rights to the trial data to B.More, Inc for a nominal sum, and a co-author reported two patents issued by Reset Pharmaceuticals. Certainty: low. Status: single study.
claim.population: Adults aged 25 to 65 with DSM-IV alcohol dependence and at least 4 heavy drinking days in the 30 days before screening, not in treatment, without major psychiatric or other drug use disorders and with no hallucinogen use in the past year or more than 25 lifetime uses, recruited through local media at two US academic centres, 2014 to 2020 (95 randomized, 93 treated; mean age 45.8; 42 women; 75 non-Hispanic White; Bogenschutz et al., 2022)
claim.exposure: Psilocybin given by clinicians within structured psychotherapy: two 8-hour sessions (trial conditions: 25 mg/70 kg, then 30 or 40 mg/70 kg, by mouth) within 12 sessions of motivational interviewing and cognitive behavioural therapy
claim.comparator: Diphenhydramine as an active placebo (50 mg, then 100 mg) with the same psychotherapy, allocated at random
claim.outcome: Percentage of heavy drinking days over the 32 weeks after the first dose, from timeline follow-back interviews (primary); drinks per day and other exploratory drinking outcomes; guesses of the medication; adverse events
claim.magnitude: Bogenschutz et al. (2022), 48 against 45: heavy drinking days 9.71% against 23.57% over weeks 5 to 36, difference 13.86 percentage points (95% CI 3.00 to 24.72), Hedges g 0.52 (0.11 to 0.94), P = .01, decomposed from a multivariate test across three drinking outcomes (F1,86 = 6.18, P = .02); before any medication, decreases of 32.37 (23.68 to 41.07) and 27.26 (20.83 to 33.69) points from screening to the 4 weeks before dosing; drinks per day 1.17 against 2.26, difference 1.09 (0.27 to 1.92); no heavy drinking days 16/48 against 5/45, odds ratio 4 (1.32 to 12.10); no drinking in weeks 5 to 36 11/48 against 4/45, odds ratio 3.05 (0.89 to 10.40); no drinking in weeks 33 to 36 23/48 against 11/45, odds ratio 2.84 (1.17 to 6.89); correct guesses after 93.6% and 94.7% of sessions (participants) and 92.4% and 97.4% (therapists); headache within 48 hours 21/48 against 2/45; serious adverse events 0 against 3.
claim.rating_reasoning: Rated on one randomized trial: randomized evidence starts high; down one level for risk of bias (self-reported drinking by participants who almost all knew their allocation) and one for imprecision (93 people, an interval from 3.00 to 24.72 points, a trial stopped early): low. 'Is associated with' because the certainty is low (METHODS §6.1). Status single study: one trial, not replicated among the sources read. The fall in the psilocybin group's heavy drinking days from screening to follow-up (56.48% to 9.71%, an 83% fall by editors' arithmetic) is not used as an effect: most of it came before any medication, in both groups. No doses are given beyond the trial conditions, and the sedative given for anxiety is named without its dose. The smoking pilot this answer used to include is now a separate answer, rated on its own evidence (very low), because GRADE rates certainty per outcome.

questions_now.q: Did the US government's anti-drug ads stop teens using cannabis?
Did the US government's anti-drug ads stop teens using cannabis?

lines_now.short: No sign they did. Congress put nearly $1 billion into the campaign, but teen cannabis use stayed flat, and teens who remembered more ads weren't less likely to start.
lines_now.but: Nearly every teen saw the ads, so there was no group without them to compare cannabis use with.
how: A national survey interviewed 8,117 US kids aged 9 to 18 at home, and many again up to three times, between 1999 and 2004.
94 in 100 remembered seeing anti-drug ads at least monthly. About 24 in 100 teens had ever used cannabis, in 2000 and again in 2004.
Teens who remembered more ads were no less likely to start cannabis by the next interview, and fewer said they definitely wouldn't.
In one of three periods, more ads even went with more first use of cannabis. The authors call this tentative, not definitive.
lines_now.rate: One national survey followed US teens from 1999 to 2004. Almost every teen saw the ads, so no group without them could be compared, and teens reported their own ad viewing and cannabis use.

claim.statement: In US youths aged 12.5 to 18 in a national household panel (the National Survey of Parents and Youth: three cohorts aged 9 to 18 from a probability sample of US households, interviewed at home four times between November 1999 and June 2004; 8,117 youths in the first round, with a 65% response rate, and 5,126 in the fourth), more recalled exposure to the US National Youth Anti-Drug Media Campaign compared with less recalled exposure did not detectably reduce marijuana (cannabis) use or first use, or strengthen antidrug intentions, beliefs, norms or confidence in refusing marijuana (Hornik et al., 2008). Congress appropriated nearly $1 billion for the campaign for 1998–2004; it bought advertising from September 1999 to June 2004, 64% of its rating points on TV and radio. The evaluation was mandated by Congress and paid from the campaign's appropriation, supervised by the National Institute on Drug Abuse, which also funded the authors. There was no unexposed group: 94% of youths recalled at least one antidrug ad a month, so the evaluation compared youths who recalled more with youths who recalled less, after propensity-score weighting on more than 150 candidate confounders. Self-reported marijuana use among youths aged 12.5 to 18 did not change from 2000 to 2004: lifetime use 23.6% and 23.5% (change −0.1 percentage points, 95% CI −2.9 to 2.8) and past-30-day use 7.8% and 8.2% (0.4, −1.4 to 2.2), weighted percentages whose yearly numbers of youths are not printed; of four antidrug views among youths who had not used marijuana, only an index of beliefs and attitudes rose (6.3 points, 0.4 to 12.2). At the same interview, youths who recalled more exposure held no more antidrug views (gammas −0.02 to 0.03, every interval including no association). Among youths who had not used marijuana, more exposure went, at the next round 12 to 18 months later, with fewer saying they definitely would not use it (82.3%, 78.2% and 78.4% across rising general exposure; gamma −0.07, 95% CI −0.13 to −0.01) and with weaker antidrug norms (gamma −0.05, −0.08 to −0.02, for recall of specific ads). First use by the next round was 10.7%, 11.2% and 12.5% across rising general exposure (gamma 0.07, −0.01 to 0.15, not significant when pooled), and more first use with more exposure was significant only from the third round (July 2002 to June 2003) to the fourth (gamma 0.11, 0.00 to 0.22), which the authors call barely significant. Of 80 subgroup analyses of later outcomes, 20 were significant, 19 of them unfavourable; none of the tests is reported as corrected for multiple comparisons. The authors conclude that the campaign is unlikely to have had favourable effects, and judge the support for unfavourable effects tentative, not definitive. Exposure and use were self-reported, and with no group that missed the campaign the design cannot show what would have happened without it: effects shared by everyone, spread through friends, or occurring before the first round, which began with the full launch, would be missed. As the authors describe two school surveys, these showed some fall in youth marijuana use over these years, which this survey did not, and larger falls in tobacco and alcohol use. Certainty: low. Status: single study.
claim.population: US youths aged 12.5 to 18 at outcome measurement in the National Survey of Parents and Youth, a household panel from a stratified four-stage national probability sample (90 primary sampling units): three cohorts aged 9 to 18 interviewed at home four times, November 1999 to June 2004 (8,117, 6,516, 5,854 and 5,126 youths in rounds 1 to 4; 65% first-round response; 86% to 93% of still-eligible youths reinterviewed); association analyses restricted to youths who had not used marijuana
claim.exposure: Recalled exposure to the National Youth Anti-Drug Media Campaign's advertising: general (how often antidrug ads were seen or heard in recent months, by medium) and specific (prompted recall of up to 4 TV and 2 radio campaign ads aired in the 2 months before the interview)
claim.comparator: Youths recalling less exposure (general: under 4, 4 to 11, 12 or more a month; specific: under 1, 1 to 3, 4 to 11, 12 or more a month); no unexposed group; for trends, the same population in 2000
claim.outcome: Self-reported lifetime, past-year and past-30-day marijuana use; first use of marijuana by the next round; intention not to use marijuana, and indices of antimarijuana beliefs and attitudes, social norms and self-efficacy
claim.magnitude: Hornik et al. (2008). Trends among youths aged 12.5–18, 2000 to 2004 (weighted percentages; yearly numbers not printed): lifetime marijuana use 23.6 to 23.5 (change −0.1 percentage points, 95% CI −2.9 to 2.8); past year 17.1 to 16.7 (−0.4, −2.6 to 1.9); past 30 days 7.8 to 8.2 (0.4, −1.4 to 2.2); among youths who had not used marijuana, definitely not intending to use 86.7 to 87.5 (0.8, −1.0 to 2.6); index changes: beliefs and attitudes 6.3 (0.4 to 12.2), self-efficacy 2.4 (−3.3 to 8.2), social norms 1.2 (−5.1 to 7.3). Cross-sectional gammas −0.02 to 0.03, all intervals including 0. Lagged gammas pooled across round pairs: intention with general exposure −0.07 (−0.13 to −0.01); social norms with specific exposure −0.05 (−0.08 to −0.02); first use with general exposure 0.07 (−0.01 to 0.15) (10.7%, 11.2% and 12.5% across under 4, 4–11 and 12 or more exposures a month); first use with specific exposure printed as −0.02 (−0.13 to 0.08), although its percentages rise from 10.8% to 13.2%. First use with general exposure by round pair: 0.08 (−0.05 to 0.20), 0.01 (−0.11 to 0.13) and 0.11 (0.00 to 0.22) for rounds 1–2, 2–3 and 3–4. Subgroups: 3 of 80 cross-sectional and 20 of 80 lagged gammas significant (19 of the 20 unfavourable). No comparison with an unexposed group, so no effect of the campaign against no campaign can be given.
claim.rating_reasoning: Observational evidence (naturally occurring differences in recalled exposure within one national panel, with no unexposed group) starts low and is not rated down further, giving low. Rated as worded: no detectable favourable change with more recalled exposure, and no fall in use over the campaign years. Whether the campaign changed anything compared with no campaign is not rated, because almost every youth was exposed, which the statement says. The unfavourable associations at the next round are reported, not rated as a separate claim: they come from many tests not reported as corrected, appear only for some outcomes and periods (more first use only from round 3 to round 4), and the authors themselves judge their support tentative; the printed gamma for specific exposure and first use (−0.02) does not fit its rising percentages and is not used. Status single study: one national panel; the authors mention a smaller study of the campaign in two cities over 6 months that reported favourable effects, not read here.
