questions_now.topic: Stigma and the words we use
questions_now.q: Do words about drug use change how others see a person?
Do words about drug use change how others see a person?

lines_now.short: In one experiment, people judged 'drug use' more harshly than a 'health concern'.
lines_now.but: People rated made-up stories. No one checked how people are really treated.
how: 1,613 adults online each read one short story about a person called Alex, with the wording chosen at random. People with a drug or mental health diagnosis, or close family with one, could not take part.

When Alex's trouble was said to come from drug use, not a health concern, readers wanted more distance from Alex. They also saw Alex as more dangerous. In a pretend money task, they took a little more money from Alex, a small difference.
Calling it a 'brain disease' instead of a 'problem' made readers think more that genes or illness caused it. Its other effects were small and unclear.

An older study tested words for the person. About 500 mental health workers at two conferences agreed slightly more that a man deserved blame and punishment when he was called 'a substance abuser' than when he 'has a substance use disorder'. The difference was small and may not be reliable.
lines_now.rate: A fair test: chance decided which story each of 1,613 online volunteers read. But they answered right after reading, when people may guess what's expected, and many were young.

claim.statement: In one pre-registered online experiment with adults who said they had no substance use or psychiatric diagnosis and knew of none in a close relative, the words used to describe a person's difficulty changed some of the attitudes readers reported, but not others, and changed what they did in a pretend money task only slightly. 1,613 adults (largest age group 18 to 25; 55.9% women; 77.1% White; recruited through university research-participation schemes, Prolific and social media; country of residence not stated) were each randomly assigned to read one short story about a person called Alex. When Alex's serious trouble at home and work was said to come from increasing drug use rather than from a health concern (819 against 741 readers), readers reported wanting more social distance from Alex (standardized difference d 0.87), saw Alex as more dangerous (d 0.78) and gave higher public-stigma scores (d 0.95; means 50.6 against 42.2): two of these differences are large by the usual standard and the third (danger) is just below it. They agreed less that the condition had genetic or disease causes (d −0.35), and their hope for Alex's recovery was the same within the study's equivalence bounds (d −0.06). In a pretend task in which readers could give or take small sums of money for Alex's answers, readers of the drug-use story took slightly more money (62.05 against 53.96 pence; d 0.14, interval 0.02 to 0.26), a difference the study could not show to be larger than its 0.20 threshold for a meaningful effect, and gave the same amount within the equivalence bounds (d −0.03). Among readers of the drug-use story, calling the condition a 'chronically relapsing brain disease' rather than a 'problem' (392 against 423) made readers agree more that it had genetic or disease causes (d 0.54; the study calls this subscale blame). With the brain-disease label, social distance (d −0.20, interval −0.36 to −0.03) and public stigma (−0.18, −0.34 to −0.02) were slightly lower, and the differences in danger (−0.11) and hope (−0.07) were smaller; all four were inconclusive, so the study could not tell whether any of them was more than trivial, and the label did not reliably change the money given or taken. Framing Alex's treatment as likely to succeed rather than uncertain (the two versions also differed in whether Alex was in a treatment programme or had seen a doctor) gave inconclusive differences on every attitude measure and on money given, and the same money taken (Pennington et al., 2023). The study measured attitudes reported after one made-up story, not how people who use drugs are actually treated by the public, health workers or services; people with a substance use or psychiatric diagnosis, or a close relative with one, could not take part; in the drug-use version four questionnaire items named opioids, so that comparison changed the questions as well as the story; the intervals printed as 99% match 98% intervals; and it did not compare person-first words with labels for the person. Words for the person were tested in one earlier, smaller experiment: of 728 people at talks on substance use at two mental-health conferences in 2008 (location not stated), described by the authors as mental health care providers, 516 (mean age 51; 64.5% with a doctoral-level degree; 34.8% with a professional focus on alcohol or drug problems) completed one of two versions of a story about a man in court-ordered treatment who had positive drug and breath tests; those whose version called him 'a substance abuser' agreed slightly more with a mixed set of statements about blame, punishment, expected violence and religious or other non-medical responses than those whose version said he had 'a substance use disorder' (2.92 against 2.82 on a 1–6 scale; d about 0.2), and did not differ detectably in willingness to have him as an employee, neighbour, co-worker or friend, or in statements about treatment and biological causes (Kelly & Westerhoff, 2010). That study calls itself randomized, but the two versions were handed out alternately; 29% of those handed a form did not complete it; its printed p = .02 matches an unstated one-sided test (two-sided about .04, above the authors' own threshold of .025); and it could not rule out differences of about the same size in social contact or in the treatment and biological-cause statements. Certainty: low. Status: single study.
claim.population: Adults recruited online (university research-participation schemes, Prolific, social media; country of residence not stated; largest age group 18–25) who said they had no substance use or psychiatric diagnosis and knew of none in a close relative; 1,613 randomized; and 516 attendees of talks on substance use at two mental-health conferences in 2008, described by the authors as mental health care providers (mean age 51; 64.5% with doctoral-level degrees; 34.8% with a professional focus on alcohol or drug problems; Kelly & Westerhoff, 2010)
claim.exposure: Reading a short story in which a person's difficulty was described as drug use (against a health concern); within the drug-use story, as a 'chronically relapsing brain disease' (against a 'problem'); and treatment framed as likely to succeed, with Alex in a treatment programme (against uncertain, with Alex having seen a doctor); in the second study, a man in court-ordered treatment described as 'a substance abuser' (against as having 'a substance use disorder')
claim.comparator: Readers assigned to the other wording (at random in the pre-registered study; by alternation of the forms in Kelly & Westerhoff, 2010)
claim.outcome: Self-reported social distance, perceived danger, hope for recovery, genetic or disease attribution (the study's blame subscale), need for continued care and public stigma; rewards and punishments in a pretend money task; agreement with a mixed set of blame, punishment, expected-violence and non-medical statements, willingness for social contact, and treatment and biological-cause statements (Kelly & Westerhoff, 2010)
claim.magnitude: Pennington et al. (2023), Cohen's d with intervals printed as 99% that match 98% intervals (card reporting issue): drug use vs health concern (819 vs 741): social distance 0.87 (0.74 to 0.99), perceived danger 0.78 (0.66 to 0.90), public stigma 0.95 (0.82 to 1.07; means 50.59 vs 42.15), blame subscale (genetic or disease attribution) −0.35 (−0.47 to −0.23), all meaningful by the study's rule; prognostic optimism −0.06 (equivalent); continued care 0.09 (inconclusive); reward −0.03 (equivalent; 248.11 vs 249.72 pence); punishment 0.14 (0.02 to 0.26; inconclusive: the interval does not include zero but reaches below the 0.20 bound; 62.05 vs 53.96 pence). 'Chronically relapsing brain disease' vs 'problem' (392 vs 423, drug-use arm): blame subscale 0.54 (0.38 to 0.71; means 8.61 vs 7.22), meaningful; continued care 0.01 (equivalent); social distance −0.20 (−0.36 to −0.03), prognostic optimism −0.07, danger −0.11, public stigma −0.18 (−0.34 to −0.02; means 49.62 vs 51.20) and reward 0.15, all inconclusive; punishment 0.007 (equivalent). Treatment framed as likely to succeed vs uncertain (383 vs 362): every self-report measure and reward inconclusive (for example public stigma 0.31, 0.14 to 0.48, higher with the uncertain framing), punishment equivalent. Detectable equivalence bounds ±0.28 and ±0.30 for the label and treatment comparisons. Kelly & Westerhoff (2010), label version vs 'substance use disorder' version: 'perpetrator-punishment' subscale 2.92 (SD 0.57) vs 2.82 (SD 0.58) on a 1–6 scale, t = 2.05, 504 df, p printed as .02 (one-sided by the editors' calculation; two-sided about .041), d printed as 0.20 (about 0.17 to 0.18 recomputed; approximate 95% CI 0.01 to 0.36, editors' calculation); 'social threat' (willingness for social contact) and 'victim-treatment' (treatment, genetic and chemical-imbalance causes, severity) subscales, no difference (ps > .59).
claim.rating_reasoning: Randomized evidence starts high; down one for risk of bias and one for indirectness: low. The verb increases rests on random assignment within the experiment; the rating concerns how far the result carries to other people, other words and real treatment. The intervals printed as 99% match 98% intervals (all 24, recomputed from Table 1) and one p value is printed as below .01 when it is about .011 (card reporting issues); the study's classifications do not change. Three differences classed as inconclusive have printed intervals that do not include zero (money taken with the drug-use story; social distance and public stigma with the brain-disease label; at 99% the public-stigma interval would reach zero), and the statement gives them as small differences rather than as no change. Kelly & Westerhoff (2010), now read, adds the comparison of a label for the person with person-first wording, in one story and one sample of conference attendees: allocation by alternation and 29% non-completion give it a high risk of bias (card sc_kelly_2010: RoB 2 high), its small difference (d about 0.2, approximate 95% CI 0.01 to 0.36, editors' calculation) relies on an unstated one-sided test, and taken alone it would be rated very low; the displayed rating is set by the pre-registered study. Each contrast rests on one study and neither repeats the other, so the status stays single study. Status single study.

how_people_ask.theme: How fast do people get hooked, and can anyone use drugs without losing control?
examples: "I accidentally got addicted to opioids at 14" (r/Drugs)

questions_now.q: Do people recover from drug or alcohol problems, even without treatment?

Do people recover from drug or alcohol problems, even without treatment?

lines_now.short: Many do. For alcohol, many people who recovered were never treated.
lines_now.but: How many depends on who is counted; recovery without treatment was measured only for alcohol.
how: Of US soldiers in Vietnam, 20 in 100 said they had been dependent on narcotics there. In the year after coming home, about 1 in 100 had been. How many had treatment was not counted.
In a US survey, about 64 in 100 adults with alcohol dependence no longer had enough signs to count as dependent three years later. Some still had a few.

In 20 long studies, mostly of people who had been in treatment, and one survey, 35 to 54 in 100 were in recovery when last seen, about 17 years later on average. The researchers saw this as a slow road for many.

For alcohol, counts of recovery without treatment run from about 3 to 98 in 100, because studies count different groups. Among people who recovered, many were never treated. Among everyone with a drinking problem, fewer recover untreated within a year.
lines_now.rate: Interviews with soldiers back from Vietnam and a US national survey, plus reviews. Figures on recovery without treatment come second-hand from a review that did not check how good its 27 studies were.

freq.what: adults with alcohol dependence no longer had enough signs to count as dependent about 3 years later
freq.note: US national survey, 2001–2002 and 2004–2005; some still had one or two signs; the editors’ count from the study’s numbers, not weighted, so not a national estimate.

claim.statement: In people with alcohol or drug problems followed for between about a year and several decades, a large share no longer met the criteria for the problem at a later interview, but how many depends on who was counted (everyone with a problem, people who stayed untreated, or people who had already recovered), on how a problem, recovery ('remission') and treatment were defined, and on the length of the time window; how many recovered without treatment was measured only in studies of alcohol problems. Of 451 men interviewed from a random sample of 470 US Army enlisted men who returned from Vietnam in September 1971 (interviews 8 to 12 months after return), 43% had used narcotics there (about a third of the men had tried heroin) and 20% reported having been dependent on narcotics there (21% by the study's own criteria for dependence), against 10% who had used narcotics and 0.7% who reported dependence (1% by the criteria) since their return; of 134 men from the study's two samples who were still dependent when they left Vietnam, 50% used narcotics again after return and 14% were dependent again (the table's numbers add up to both samples together, with no weighting stated). The authors give a remission rate of 95% without saying which sample it describes; their figure, read approximately, shows that of the men first dependent in Vietnam, about 2% of 90 in the general sample and about 7% of 341 in a second sample (selected on a urine test at departure positive for narcotics, amphetamines or barbiturates) were dependent again. Remission there meant not being dependent again within about a year; many of the men counted as remitted still used narcotics, and a period of more-than-weekly narcotic use was more common after return than before Vietnam (3% against under 0.5%); men whose urine was positive at departure were to be held for detoxification and treatment, but how many men received drug treatment, before or after return, is not reported; and the authors leave open whether the men's backgrounds or the change from Vietnam to home explains the remission (Robins et al., 1975). In a US national survey of adults interviewed in 2001–2002 and again about three years later (34,653 re-interviewed), 422 of the 1,172 people who had met the criteria for alcohol dependence in the year before the first interview met them again in the year before the second (36%), so about 64% did not (1,172 = 422 + 750, an editors' sum; both shares are editors' calculations from unweighted counts in a survey that over-sampled young adults and Black and Hispanic people, so they are not national estimates); in the paper's own weighted analysis, persistence was 32.4% at ages 21–23 and 44.5% at ages 43–52. Not meeting the full criteria can include people with one or two symptoms left, and treatment between the interviews is not reported (Vergés et al., 2012). A meta-analysis of 21 studies of people with alcohol, heroin or several-drug use disorders, published 2000–2015 and mostly from the US (20 cohorts followed for 3 to 50 years, mean 17, 15 of them recruited through treatment, and one national survey that estimated remission over a lifetime), found 54% (95% CI 42% to 66%) of the people followed to the end in remission at the last follow-up, and 35% (25% to 46%) of everyone enrolled when deaths and people lost to follow-up were counted as not remitted; without the lifetime survey, about 50% (editors' recalculation) and 31%. Among the people followed to the end, single studies ranged from about 20% to 96%, the top value being the lifetime survey, and this rate, unlike the rate among everyone enrolled, was higher in cohorts followed longer and in cohorts that kept fewer of their participants. For treatment, the review compared cohorts only by whether people were in treatment when they entered, which cannot show who recovered without treatment: 51% with treatment at entry against 62% without (p 0.42), the six without including the lifetime survey (about 49% without it, editors' recalculation). Treatment during follow-up was not analysed, the pooled figures mix very different follow-up times and so describe no particular time point, the review reports no appraisal of its cohorts, and its authors read the results as showing that for many people these disorders are long-lasting (Fleury et al., 2016). For alcohol problems, a review of 124 estimates of recovery without treatment from 27 published studies (1976–2018, 24 of them North American; 71 of the estimates, the lowest among them, calculated by the reviewers from the studies' data) found figures from 2.7% to 98.3%, largely because the studies counted different things: among people already recovered, the share never treated (78% in two Canadian population surveys when recovery included moderate drinking, 56% and 66% when it meant not drinking); among people with an alcohol problem who stayed untreated, the share who recovered (in the US national survey of 2001–2002, 12.4% when recovery meant not drinking and 32.6% when moderate drinking also counted; in a Dutch survey, 78% of people with an alcohol use disorder who stayed untreated for three years were in remission at follow-up, against 40% of those whose disorder was moderate or severe; in one US cohort of people who had had no treatment beyond a single detoxification or a visit to an information and referral centre, 36.0% were in remission at both the 1- and 3-year follow-ups, and 14.0% when it also had to hold 16 years later); and among everyone with an alcohol problem, the share who recovered without treatment, which gave the lowest figures (2.7% to 63.6% in the nine studies that allowed all three counts). Most studies used a window of about one year, the review did not appraise the studies, and these figures are second-hand (Mellor et al., 2019). So a high share of never-treated people among those who recovered and a much lower share of everyone with a problem recovering without treatment in a year can both be right. No source read here measured recovery without treatment for drugs other than alcohol; for the Vietnam veterans, how many were treated is not reported. Certainty: very low. Status: replicated.
claim.population: US Army enlisted men returning from Vietnam in September 1971, interviewed 8 to 12 months later (451 in a random general sample; 898 in both samples) (Robins et al., 1975); US adults in a national household survey interviewed in 2001–2002 and 2004–2005 (34,653 re-interviewed; 1,172 of them with past-year alcohol dependence at the first interview, an editors' sum) (Vergés et al., 2012); 21 studies of people with alcohol, heroin or several-drug use disorders published 2000–2015 (20 cohorts, 15 recruited through treatment, and one national survey's lifetime estimate) (Fleury et al., 2016); 27 studies of untreated remission from alcohol problems, 1976–2018, mostly North American (Mellor et al., 2019)
claim.exposure: Having had an alcohol or drug problem (narcotic dependence in Vietnam, self-reported or by the study's own criteria; DSM-IV alcohol dependence; substance use disorders as each cohort diagnosed them; alcohol problems as each study defined them), with or without treatment as each study defined it
claim.comparator: None (descriptive); the same people's earlier status; in the alcohol review, three different denominators (everyone with a problem, people who stayed untreated, people already recovered)
claim.outcome: No longer meeting the criteria for the problem (remission) at a later interview or at the last follow-up, as each study defined it (not dependent again within about a year; not meeting full DSM-IV criteria in the year before an interview about three years later; at least six months without meeting criteria; abstinence or moderate drinking), and the share of it without treatment
claim.magnitude: Robins et al. (1975), general sample N=451, before / in / since Vietnam: narcotic use 11% / 43% / 10%; dependence self-reported 0.2% / 20% / 0.7%, by the study's criteria 0.4% / 21% / 1%. Still dependent at departure (both samples pooled, no weighting stated, n=134): 50% used narcotics after return, 14% dependent again. A period of more-than-weekly narcotic use since return 3% vs under 0.5% before service. Men first dependent in Vietnam dependent again 8–10 months after return (Figure, approximate): about 2% (general sample, N=90) and about 7% (urine-positive sample, N=341). Stated remission rate 95% (no denominator). Vergés et al. (2012), NESARC 2001–2002 to 2004–2005: 422 of 1,172 with past-year alcohol dependence (36%) dependent again about three years later, about 64% (750) not (1,172 = 422 + 750, and both shares are editors' calculations, unweighted); weighted persistence 32.4% (ages 21–23) and 44.5% (43–52). Fleury et al. (2016), 21 studies (20 cohorts, follow-up 3–50 years, and one lifetime survey estimate entered as 95.7%): standard remission 54.4% (95% CI 42.1–66.2), studies 19.6–95.7%, I² 99.4%; conservative 35.0% (25.2–46.4), I² 99.5%; without the lifetime survey, standard about 50.1% (42.5–57.6; editors' recalculation from Fig. 4, matching the lowest printed leave-one-out value) and conservative 30.9% (26.1–36.1, printed); treatment at baseline 51.1% vs not 62.4% (standard rate, p 0.421; about 48–49% for the five cohorts without treatment at baseline other than the lifetime survey, editors' recalculation; the printed conservative-rate subgroups could not be rebuilt from Fig. 4); standard rate higher with longer follow-up (B 0.046 per year, p 0.004) and lower retention (p 0.016), neither for the conservative rate. Mellor et al. (2019), alcohol, 124 estimates (71 calculated by the reviewers): 2.7% to 98.3%; nine studies with all three methods: all people with a problem 2.7–63.6%, untreated people 6.5–77.9%, remitted people 4.3–94.2% (6.4% with Table 3's values) (unweighted medians 12.4, 38.9 and 43.9, not rates); 78% of remitted people untreated (two Canadian surveys; abstinence or moderate drinking; 56.0% and 65.7% with abstinence only); 12.4% vs 32.6% of untreated people remitted (abstinence vs abstinence or moderate drinking; NESARC); 78% vs 40% of people untreated for three years in remission (any vs moderate or severe disorder; Netherlands); 36.0% vs 14.0% (remission at both 1 and 3 years vs also at 16 years; the 14.0% a reviewers' calculation; a US cohort).
claim.rating_reasoning: Descriptive claim: starts low and is rated as a description of the samples. Down one for risk of bias, because the part of the question about recovery without treatment rests on second-hand, unappraised estimates (and on a meta-analysis of unappraised, mostly treatment-recruited cohorts): very low. A lenient reading would rate the Vietnam and national-survey figures alone (primary data from a near-complete random sample and a weighted national survey) as low for the narrower statement that many people no longer meet the criteria within one to three years; the rating is set by the weakest necessary link. Not upgraded (descriptive). Status replicated: the direction holds in independent samples (Vietnam veterans; the US national survey; the cohorts pooled by Fleury et al.), but the US national survey appears in four places (Vergés et al.; two of the studies pooled by Fleury et al., the lifetime estimate and Moss et al., 2010, a general-population sample from the same survey followed for three years; and Dawson et al. in Mellor et al.), which are not counted as independent of each other. Not used: the 95% remission rate as a figure (no stated denominator), Fleury et al.'s annual remission rates (inconsistent with its pooled proportions), its 14 years of use before remission (not derivable from its table) and its conservative-rate comparison by treatment at entry (not reproducible from its study values), and Mellor et al.'s medians as rates (card reporting issues). The comparison of cohorts by treatment at entry describes who entered each study, not who recovered without treatment.

questions_now.q: Can drinking lots of water on MDMA lead to low blood salt?

lines_now.short: Some young people were treated for low blood salt (sodium) after taking MDMA.
lines_now.but: These are reports of people who became ill, so they cannot show how often it happens.
how: In 17 people aged 15 to 26 reported to a UK poisons service, at least 10 had drunk a lot of fluid. Two died; each had taken one tablet, had drunk a lot of water, and drank or was given more after feeling ill.
In California poison-centre records, 73 of 188 people who had their blood salt measured had a low level, and 4 of those 73 died.
The papers think MDMA makes the body hold on to water, which waters down the salt in the blood; the UK authors say how it does this is not yet known.
No paper compared amounts of MDMA or of fluid between people, so none can show whether taking more makes it more likely.
lines_now.rate: Records from two poison services, in the UK and California, which agree. But MDMA was confirmed by tests in only some cases, and in California only about a third had blood salt measured.

claim.statement: After MDMA, a fall in blood sodium (below 130 mmol/L) with seizures and brain swelling has been reported in mostly young people within hours of taking the drug, in two case series from poison services and in published case reports. These describe a pattern but cannot say how often it happens, because they count only people who became ill and came to a poison service or hospital. In 17 patients aged 15 to 26 (7 men, 10 women) reported to a UK poisons service over 28 months (Hartung et al., 2002), sodium on the first day was 107 to 128 mmol/L and all had become ill within 12 hours of taking the drug. A large amount of fluid, alcoholic or not, was known to have been drunk by 10 of the 17 (8 of the 15 who recovered and both who died; editors' count); for 5 of the 15 who recovered the fluid history was not available. Of those 15, 10 had seizures and 13 were recorded as recovering completely; of the 13 with a stated amount of MDMA, 12 had taken 2 or fewer tablets (half a tablet to three), and temperature at hospital was recorded as normal in 12 (37.5 degrees Celsius in two, 34.8 in one). Two patients died after brain swelling, a 15-year-old and an 18-year-old, both female, each after one tablet and each having taken MDMA before: one had drunk at least 3 litres of water while dancing, the other water from about two hours after the tablet, with some alcohol; both were given or drank more water after they began to feel ill, arrived at hospital at 32.6 and 33 degrees, and had blood MDMA of 0.05 and 0.209 mg/l. The UK authors note that people had at first been advised to drink plenty of fluids to prevent overheating. In California poison-centre records for 2000 to 2005 (Rosenson et al., 2007), 73 of 188 people with a recorded sodium (about 39 in 100) had a level below 130 mmol/L; 13 of the 545 included cases died, 4 of them in the low-sodium group, all with brain swelling on CT scan and low blood pressure needing medicines. Hyperthermia was recorded in 40 of the 545 (7.3 in 100) and did not differ clearly between people with and without low sodium (odds ratios 0.58 in women and 0.29 in men, both intervals including 1). In that series MDMA exposure rests on the history given (35 of 103 urine screens were negative for amphetamines but still counted), and the paper gives neither the amount of fluid nor the amount of MDMA. A narrative review of published case reports (Campbell & Rosner, 2008; second-hand, and its table of 32 cases draws 10 rows from the California series) describes more than 25 reports with sodium 101 to 130 mEq/L, most in females aged 15 to 30 after a single dose, including one in which sodium fell from 136 to 130 after 1700 ml of water was drunk following five tablets. A later narrative review (Faria et al., 2020; second-hand, PubMed searched to October 2019 with one author mainly responsible) has 52 table rows about phenethylamine-associated cases, 50 labelled MDMA, and 21 outcomes labelled death. The 36 rows with sodium have lowest values 101–130 mmol/L; one of those rows also reports an earlier value 137, not an extra case. Two pairs of rows appear to repeat cases, although the primary reports were not read; one case cites an unrelated laboratory-methods paper; three fatal rows report neither a numeric sodium result nor hyponatraemia among their effect labels; and one outcome is blank despite a death in the cited title. The authorless 2001 case is traceable, while another row's compound label conflicts with its reference title. Ten fatal rows come from the California series, so the review must not be added to it as an independent 52-person series. Amounts are unknown or blank in 30 rows, including 14 of 21 fatal rows. The review's single-dose statement is restricted to most reported deaths or permanent neurological injuries in women aged 15–30; its table cannot verify that statement. In the 10 fatal rows with sodium, values 109–126 mmol/L lie within the 101–130 range of lowest per-row values in the 24 recovery rows with sodium (editors' counts). The papers explain the fall by MDMA making the body release the water-holding hormone vasopressin, so that water is held back and drinking beyond the body's needs dilutes the sodium; the hormone rise is described from other studies not read here, and the UK authors write that the mechanism remains to be established. Faria also proposes sodium loss in sweat, while describing the drinking reports as anecdotal and the mechanisms as not fully understood. None of the papers read here compared amounts of MDMA or of fluid between people, and the 2020 review bases its drinking discussion on anecdotal reports, so they cannot show whether taking more changes the risk. Blood sodium was not measured in the controlled laboratory sessions of healthy volunteers (Vizeli & Liechti, 2017).
claim.population: Mostly young people who became ill after taking ecstasy (MDMA) and came to a poison service or hospital: 17 patients aged 15 to 26 reported to a UK poisons service over 28 months (1993 to 1996); 545 poison-centre cases in California in 2000 to 2005 (mean age 21), 188 of them with a measured sodium; and published case reports as described in two narrative reviews (more than 25 reports to 2008; 52 tabulated cases to 2018, with errors)
claim.exposure: MDMA sold as ecstasy tablets, content unknown (MDMA confirmed by laboratory tests in 8 of the 15 UK survivors and in both who died; in California by history, with urine screens in 103 of 188 and no specific method), with fluid intake recorded only for some: a large amount in 10 of the 17 UK patients; stated amounts of half a tablet to three tablets in 13 UK survivors; one published case took five tablets (study conditions as reported, not recommendations)
claim.comparator: None for the UK series and the case reports; in California, cases with a sodium of 130 mmol/L or more or reported as normal (115 of 188)
claim.outcome: Serum sodium below 130 mmol/L, seizures, coma, brain swelling, death, and the temperature recorded at hospital
claim.magnitude: UK poisons service, 17 patients over 28 months (Hartung): day 1 sodium 107 to 128 mmol/l; symptoms within 12 hours of the drug in all; large fluid intake known in 10 (8 of the 15 who recovered and both who died), history not available for 5 of the 15; seizures in 10 of the 15 who recovered; 13 of the 15 recorded as recovering completely; temperature at hospital normal in 12 of 15 (37.5 in two, 34.8 in one); 12 of 13 with a stated amount took 2 or fewer tablets (half a tablet to 3); 6 with biochemistry typical of excess antidiuretic hormone; 2 deaths (aged 15 and 18, both female, one tablet each, blood MDMA 0.05 and 0.209 mg/l, temperature 32.6 and 33 degrees Celsius at hospital). California poison control, 545 included cases 2000 to 2005 (Rosenson): sodium recorded in 188 (34.5%); below 130 mmol/L in 73 (about 39 in 100; the text once says 74), median 122 (25th to 75th percentile 119 to 124); 13 deaths in 545 (2.4%), 4 of them in the low-sodium group, all with brain swelling on CT and low blood pressure needing medicines; hyperthermia in 40 of 545 (7.3%), odds ratio for hyperthermia with low sodium against without 0.58 (0.15 to 2.17) in women and 0.29 (0.04 to 2.40) in men; rave party the recorded site for 50 of 545 (9.1%), including 3 of 74 low-sodium cases. Narrative review (Campbell), second-hand: more than 25 case reports, sodium 101 to 130 mEq/L; 32 tabulated cases, 16 deaths. Narrative review (Faria), second-hand: Table 3 has 52 rows (1991–2018), not verified unique cases: 46 female, 21 labelled deaths, 27 recoveries, 3 unknown and 1 blank outcome. Lowest sodium in 36 rows is 101–130 mmol/L, including one with an earlier value 137; 10 fatal rows have 109–126, within the 101–130 range of lowest per-row values in 24 recovery rows. Amount is unknown/blank in 30 rows, including 14/21 fatal rows. Probable duplicates, citation mismatches and unconfirmed fatal low-sodium labels limit interpretation; 10 fatal rows overlap the California series. No rate of low sodium among people who take MDMA can be derived from these counts.
claim.rating_reasoning: Case series start low (observational, no comparison group for the UK series). Risk of bias -1 and imprecision -1 give very low; descriptive claims are never upgraded for a large effect (METHODS 6.3). The claim states what was recorded in two poison-service series and, as described in a narrative review, in published case reports, and that none could give a rate. Status replicated: two independent services in two countries show the same pattern; the 2008 review adds nothing independent, because its table draws on the California series and appears to include a UK case that is also in the first series, and the 2020 review (Faria et al.) is not an independent 52-person cohort: its table draws 10 of its 21 labelled deaths from the California series and contains errors (card sc_faria_2020), so it is cited for what it tabulates, with the errors stated. The vasopressin explanation is reported as the papers' explanation and as untested here; it is not part of what the claim asserts. No advice on fluid or on amounts is given.
